st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source does not assess self-representation, filing growth, litigant outcomes, or shifted costs to courts and opponents. It redirects attention to a related but materially different priority: preserving lawyers’ and law students’ substantive reasoning through bounded, independently assessable AI use.
qs: Part I surveys the existing literature on AI’s actual and anticipated influence on legal practice, with particular attention to the concern that AI use may erode lawyers’ substantive understanding of the law.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source reports only an attrition check on participant comparability and explicitly limits category-level comparison because few participants dropped out. It does not address whether enthusiasm establishes investment value or the cluster’s broader implementation conditions, benefits or risks.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The excerpt consists mainly of footnote citations and does not address whether cheaper AI assistance increases self-representation, improves remedies, shifts burdens to courts, or expands population-level access. Its references to an adoption gap and legal-tool reliability are adjacent to the cluster’s concerns but do not establish a discernible position on its central proposition.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source aligns with two subsidiary points: AI can improve performance on some legal tasks, while overreliance may impair lawyers’ critical analysis. But it focuses on professional legal work and industry transformation, not the cluster’s central access-to-justice dispute over lower-cost consumer assistance, UPL boundaries, provider reform, or protections for self-represented users.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core position that lawyers remain responsible for independently verifying AI-assisted work and that technical safeguards do not replace professional judgment. It materially extends the governance rationale by identifying a longer-term risk: AI-mediated work may weaken lawyers’ internalisation of legal reasoning and leave latent issues undetected, supporting measured, task-sensitive integration rather than prohibition.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts that AI exposure or improved output does not itself establish professional readiness, and materially develops the proposition with randomized evidence showing conditional effects on unaided reasoning. It also translates that evidence into concrete guidance: AI use should remain bounded by the user’s capacity to assess, explain and extend the output independently.
qs: These findings suggest that AI does not inevitably erode or promote independent legal reasoning, but that its effects depend on when and how law students and junior lawyers use AI.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s evidence-backed account of task-dependent productivity gains and its preference for bounded, human-supervised use. It materially extends that position by identifying possible erosion of independent legal reasoning as a distinct longer-term risk and prescribing use only where lawyers can independently assess the output, within narrow project components and suitable working conditions. It does not directly establish the cluster’s consumer-side claim that risk shifts to unrepresented users.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s expertise-pipeline concern and materially develops it by distinguishing AI assistance on already-understood material from cognitive outsourcing that undermines legal judgment. It also proposes adapting existing law-firm training for critical assessment of AI, though it does not independently establish the cluster’s broader claims about leverage, revenue or workforce contraction.
qs: Law firms that for decades have trained their lawyers to assess each others’ advice should be able to develop similar training for assessing advice from AI.

st.t: Legal productivity: Speed gains exceed quality gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-dependent account of AI assistance and materially extends it by showing that, for legal synthesis, substantive quality gains can be unusually large alongside a smaller time reduction, with stronger initial synthesis supporting later unaided reasoning. It therefore qualifies—but does not reject—the general pattern that speed gains are more consistent than quality gains.
qs: We also observe an increase of more than one standard deviation (1.08 standard deviations) in substantive quality.
These results suggest that AI’s ability to improve subsequent legal reasoning operates indirectly, by improving the quality of initial work on which subsequent work builds.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster with randomized evidence that bounded AI assistance can improve immediate synthesis and later unaided legal application, while also identifying competence risks when AI revision dilutes stronger work. Its short-term, human-in-the-loop findings support selective use, verification and caution rather than lawyer replacement or inevitable deskilling.
qs: In other words, AI use on the initial synthesis task improved overall performance on the later application task by 24.01%.
Contrary to our expectations, while AI use during the revision stage helped participants improve weak reasoning memos, it also led participants with strong reasoning memos to make those memos worse.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source accepts the need for active scrutiny and materially extends it beyond hallucination, confidentiality and output verification to the risk that AI reliance may erode legal reasoning, judgment and long-term professional capacity. It supports this concern with non-legal experiments while expressly acknowledging limited direct evidence in legal settings.
qs: Over the long term, such gaps could translate into diminished professional capacity in settings where AI is unavailable, constrained, or simply less helpful.45      Although there is limited empirical evidence regarding these potentially negative consequences of AI use in the legal setting, there is mounting evidence demonstrating that it exists in other settings.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source endorses selective, task-bounded augmentation and materially strengthens the cluster with randomized evidence: AI improved synthesis and later unaided application, but could degrade initially strong work during revision. It therefore supports retaining independent judgment and limiting AI use to outputs lawyers can critically assess, explain and own, while leaving long-term developmental effects unresolved.
qs: These findings suggest that AI does not inevitably erode or promote independent legal reasoning, but that its effects depend on when and how law students and junior lawyers use AI.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts bounded AI productivity and task-level assistance while materially developing the cluster’s competence and governance account: complementarity depends on lawyers retaining enough independent understanding to question, explain and modify AI output, with training designed to preserve that judgment over time.
qs: Taken together, these developments suggest that the legal profession will increasingly confront practical questions about how best to integrate AI into legal work, including which tasks are most amenable to AI assistance and whether reliance on AI poses risks to short-term work quality or long-term skill development.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment framing and materially strengthens it with preregistered causal evidence. It shows large gains on a bounded synthesis task without short-term comprehension loss, while finding that AI revision can help weaker work but degrade stronger work. Its recommendations make task decomposition, user expertise, verification time and cognitive conditions central to safe deployment, directly developing the cluster’s account of jagged capability and meaningful oversight.
qs: In other words, AI usage improved overall productivity by 92.36%.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core position that AI may assist legal work only while lawyers retain active professional judgment and substantive critical analysis. Its warning against overreliance reinforces the need for meaningful human supervision, though the excerpt offers neither a developed argument about filing rules nor empirical evidence.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central concern that legal education must preserve independent reasoning while addressing AI competence. It specifically warns that exclusive or heavy AI dependence may weaken comprehension and legal judgment, while appropriately framing the legal effects as a question requiring empirical study. Because the supplied excerpt gives no trial results, it does not resolve the cluster’s disputes over timing, restrictions, or long-term learning effects.
qs: But most will share the intuition that the students who trained entirely on AI-generated texts will not learn the reasoning skills that they need to succeed on exams and in practice.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between fabricated citations and misleading uses of genuine authorities. It also affirms that lawyers must verify authorities for existence, accuracy and relevance, while warning that rapid AI-assisted drafting can amplify substantive legal errors. Its separate confidentiality discussion is consistent with the cluster’s view that citation safeguards do not resolve other risks.
qs: More subtly, it can also include references to genuine decisions that do not support the propositions for which they are cited, or attribution of fabricated quotations to authentic sources.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s expertise-development concern by predicting that AI-assisted productivity can reduce engagement with underlying legal sources and weaken later unaided reasoning. It supplies a theoretical mechanism rather than empirical legal-study results and does not address the cluster’s broader accountability and regulatory issues.
qs: By reducing the level of cognitive engagement with the underlying sources, we predict that lawyers experience a decline in their own independent ability to engage in reasoning tasks.
This results in a tradeoff: AI use increases productivity on tasks while impairing performance on subsequent tasks when AI is no longer available.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that legal AI remains useful but unreliable and requires verification. It specifically recognises both fabricated authorities and subtler misuses of genuine sources, while warning that cite-checking and other safeguards mitigate rather than eliminate errors, especially during rapid AI-assisted drafting.
qs: More subtly, it can also include references to genuine decisions that do not support the propositions for which they are cited, or attribution of fabricated quotations to authentic sources.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious assessment that legal AI adoption and reported efficiency gains have not yet established broad workforce displacement. It reinforces the distinction between transformative potential, actual adoption and anecdotal reports, though it does not specifically substantiate the claim that junior training pipelines face the sharpest risk.
qs: Although systematic evidence from practicing attorneys is less available for a variety of reasons, a growing number of practicing lawyers report that their practices have been fundamentally transformed by their embrace of AI.
At the same time, these anecdotal claims are not necessarily reliable.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s workflow-sensitive, measurement-focused proposition by separating AI-assisted memo production from unaided comprehension and by examining differential attrition as a potential threat to inference. However, the supplied excerpts report methods rather than productivity, quality or comprehension outcomes, so they do not establish whether AI saved time, improved work or impaired learning.

Ultimately, we find no evidence that differential attrition affected the balance of the experiment.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious, situated account of professional change: it reports practitioner claims of transformation but stresses that systematic evidence is limited and anecdotes may be unreliable. It therefore reinforces the cluster’s rejection of confident sector-wide conclusions, although it provides little direct analysis of professional power, status or organisational boundary work.
qs: Although systematic evidence from practicing attorneys is less available for a variety of reasons, a growing number of practicing lawyers report that their practices have been fundamentally transformed by their embrace of AI.
At the same time, these anecdotal claims are not necessarily reliable.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source endorses a supervised, bounded copilot model in which lawyers independently understand, assess and defend AI-assisted work. It also supports the cluster’s concern that verification and responsible oversight can erode efficiency gains, particularly when AI delegation weakens legal reasoning or exceeds the lawyer’s expertise, while acknowledging productivity benefits and limited long-term evidence.
qs: If the answer is no, the task has likely been delegated rather than assisted, and the professional and developmental costs of that delegation may outweigh its efficiency gains.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI does not displace professional judgment and that verification must assess whether authorities substantively support the work, not merely whether citations exist. It reinforces this with an independent-defensibility test while treating skill erosion and performance decline as qualified risks rather than universal findings.
qs: A useful heuristic is to ask, before relying on AI-generated work product, whether the lawyer could defend that work product in a demanding conversation with a skeptical colleague or judge without further preparation.

kp.d: The authors describe a gap, as of early 2026, between evidence of AI's technical capabilities and its practical influence on legal practice. They report continued reluctance among lawyers, judges and clients, and identify hallucinations, confidentiality and erosion of professional reasoning as central perceived risks, alongside social, economic and regulatory factors.
qs: Even among lawyers who incorporate AI into their work, most continue to treat it as a limited tool, rather than as a transformative technology that fundamentally alters how they practice law.
These perceived risks fall into three categories: that AI will hallucinate source material,
that reliance on AI will erode human legal reasoning and professional judgment.

kp.k: Earlier evidence supports task-specific productivity gains
kp.d: Reviewing prior studies rather than reporting this experiment's results, the authors describe a late-2024 randomized trial finding statistically significant productivity gains on five of six legal tasks, ranging roughly from 50 to 130 percent through quality and speed improvements. A mid-2023 trial reported tasks completed between 5 and 38 percent more quickly, without statistically significant quality improvement. They distinguish these human-assistance experiments from autonomous-output benchmarks and note limited rigorous evidence from practicing attorneys.
qs: Another randomized controlled trial in mid-2023 found that participants with access to an earlier AI model completed lawyering tasks between 5 and 38 percent more quickly than those in the control group.
Unfortunately, rigorous empirical evidence regarding the impact on practicing attorneys of adopting AI technologies is limited.

kp.k: Experiment tests sequential, supervised AI use
kp.d: The October 2025 remote experiment analyzed 91 second- and third-year University of Minnesota law students: 50 AI-exposed participants and 41 controls. Within one three-hour sitting, participants synthesized a closed source packet, answered a closed-book comprehension quiz, applied the law to facts and revised their application memo. Only the treatment group used Gemini 2.5 Pro for synthesis; neither group could use AI for comprehension or application; both used it for revision. The treatment concerned initial exposure to AI synthesis, not a standardized duration of use.
qs: We recruited 91 second- and third-year students from the University of Minnesota Law School.

Accordingly, the treatment in our study is defined as the initial exposure to the AI-generated synthesis rather than the amount of time participants spent using Gemini 2.5 Pro during the synthesis task.

kp.k: Closed materials and verification structured the intervention
kp.d: The assignment concerned servitudes burdening personal property, using a twelve-page packet of edited Restatement provisions and four researcher-written opinions from a hypothetical jurisdiction. Participants had 75 minutes for synthesis, ten for a six-question comprehension quiz, 60 for application and 20 for revision. Structured synthesis instructions required checking AI output against the packet. A single experienced legal-writing professor graded all 273 anonymized, randomized memos using preregistered rubrics.
qs: The source packet was twelve pages long.
Step 3: Check AI Output. Carefully review the materials in the source packet to check the accuracy of the AI-produced output. Correct any errors.

Finally, all memos were fully anonymized and randomized before grading, so that the grader did not know whether the participant was in the control or treatment group, or how the participant performed on any other tasks.

kp.d: Synthesis overall quality averaged 10.60 for AI-exposed participants versus 6.63 for controls, an increase of 3.97 points or 59.78% (p<0.001). Substantive quality increased 65.03%, organization 67.49% and polish 48.10%, each p<0.001. The authors report overall and substantive effects of 1.20 and 1.08 sample standard deviations respectively. These gains therefore concerned substance as well as presentation; explanations involving model advances or task suitability remain possibilities.
qs: On average, participants in the control group scored 6.63 points, whereas those in the AI-exposed group scored 10.60 points.
We also observe an increase of more than one standard deviation (1.08 standard deviations) in substantive quality.
This indicates that AI is improving both form and substance.

kp.k: Synthesis became faster and more productive
kp.d: AI-exposed participants reported taking 60.70 minutes for synthesis versus 69.46 minutes for controls, a reduction of 8.76 minutes or 12.62% (p<0.001). Productivity, defined as rubric quality points divided by minutes rather than revenue or billable output, rose 92.36% (p<0.001). Regression controls for GPA, class year and prior AI usage did not meaningfully change the reported productivity results.
qs: In other words, AI usage reduced the time spent on the synthesis task by nine minutes or 12.62%.
In other words, AI usage improved overall productivity by 92.36%.

kp.k: Immediate comprehension showed no significant difference
kp.d: Contrary to the preregistered prediction of impaired comprehension, controls averaged 3.86 correct answers and AI-exposed participants 3.88 on the six-question closed-book quiz (p=0.935). The authors limit this finding to comprehension assessed soon after exposure; it does not establish durable learning effects.
qs: On average, participants in the control group scored 3.86 points, whereas those in the AI-exposed group scored 3.88 points.

These findings therefore provide no evidence that AI assistance undermines participants’ comprehension of the underlying legal materials when comprehension is assessed soon after exposure to the materials.

kp.k: Earlier AI use improved subsequent unaided application
kp.d: Although neither group could use AI during application, participants could consult their synthesis memos. AI-exposed participants averaged 6.56 overall quality points versus 5.29 for controls, a 24.01% improvement (p=0.02), or 0.49 sample standard deviations. Depth of analysis improved 27.15% (p=0.04) and organization 24.75% (p=0.01); the 20.45% increase in focus and emphasis was not statistically significant (p=0.10). Results contradicted the predicted downstream impairment and persisted with background controls.
qs: Participants had access to their prior synthesis memo and were instructed to save time by not repeating its contents.
In other words, AI use on the initial synthesis task improved overall performance on the later application task by 24.01%.
We observe an increase of nearly half a standard deviation (0.49 standard deviations) in overall performance on the application task.

kp.k: Stronger foundational memos suggest an indirect mechanism
kp.d: After controlling for synthesis quality, the AI-exposure coefficient on application quality was no longer statistically significant. A one-standard-deviation increase in synthesis performance was associated with a 0.76-point application increase. The authors interpret this as suggesting that better foundational work supported later reasoning, while proposing further experiments to separate that instrumental benefit from cognitive effects of initial AI use.
qs: Once we control for participants’ performance on the synthesis task, the AI-exposed treatment is no longer statistically significant.
A one standard deviation increase (3.30) in synthesis-task performance is associated with a 0.76 point increase on the application task.
These results suggest that AI’s ability to improve subsequent legal reasoning operates indirectly, by improving the quality of initial work on which subsequent work builds.

kp.k: Application productivity gains were not statistically significant
kp.d: AI-exposed participants took 53.13 minutes for application versus 49.63 for controls, 3.50 minutes or 7.10% longer (p=0.09). Application productivity increased 13.20%, but not significantly (p=0.202). The authors therefore identify a possible quality-speed trade-off at application, while reporting that the AI-exposed group completed synthesis and application together an average of 5.26 minutes faster.
qs: On average, participants in the AI-exposed group took longer to draft their application memos than participants in the control group.
Although participants in the AI-exposed group produced higher quality memos, they took slightly longer to complete the task.
Between the synthesis and application tasks, participants in the AI-exposed group completed the whole study an average of 5.26 minutes faster than participants in the control group.

kp.k: AI revision improved weaker work but degraded stronger work
kp.d: All participants used AI to revise their independently written application memos, despite instructions not to alter substance. Weaker initial memos generally improved while stronger ones deteriorated. The paper reports estimated changes of +1.91 points for initial scores of three and −8.08 points for initial scores of fourteen. Initial treatment assignment did not significantly distinguish revision outcomes. Strong initial performers nevertheless continued to produce stronger revised work than weak initial performers.
qs: Participants whose initial memos were relatively weak produced stronger memos after revising with AI.
Surprisingly, however, participants whose initial memos were relatively strong produced weaker memos after revising with AI.
High-performing participants continued to produce stronger work than lower-performing participants even after revision.

kp.d: The authors propose that AI may flatten nuanced analysis, and that time pressure, cognitive fatigue or unwarranted deference may encourage acceptance of harmful edits. They do not establish which mechanism explains the revision pattern. Stronger initial performers spent more, not less, time revising, which the authors regard as inconsistent with an explanation based simply on spending less time reviewing edits.
qs: One possible explanation is that AI produces a leveling effect by improving weaker drafts while standardizing or flattening stronger ones.
Alternatively, participants may have deferred to the AI’s suggestions, failing to critically consider whether they meaningfully improved the overall memo.
Participants who produced higher-quality memos on the application task spent more time on the revision task.

kp.k: Reliability findings do not eliminate hallucination risks
kp.d: The authors observed very few fabricated or misstated rules in either group and no evidence that AI-exposed participants were more prone to the identified error. They restrict the implication to supervised synthesis of closed materials, not open-ended legal research. More broadly, they argue that checking authorities can mitigate hallucinations and enterprise safeguards can address confidentiality, whereas safeguarding professional reasoning is harder to routinize.
qs: We observed very few fabricated or misstated legal rules in either group.
The absence of hallucinations in our study should not be interpreted as evidence that AI models no longer hallucinate.
Rather, our results show that AI outputs can be reliable for summarizing a closed set of documents when properly supervised.

kp.d: The study covers only one three-hour session and does not determine whether sustained AI reliance erodes or improves skills over months or years. The authors report cross-domain studies suggesting reduced engagement, recall or independent performance as grounds for concern, not direct evidence of long-term legal deskilling. They also acknowledge that repeated use could improve users' ability to work with AI.
qs: This design cannot capture the long-term cognitive consequences of repeated AI reliance over months or years.
Skill erosion, if it occurs, is likely to be cumulative and gradual rather than immediate.
Conversely, repeated exposure to AI may allow individuals to use it more skillfully, improving their overall ability to synthesize legal materials and apply them to specific fact patterns.

kp.k: Generalization beyond the experiment is constrained
kp.d: The authors qualify their findings by the single-school student sample, closed hypothetical materials, artificial task segmentation, specified model and prompting, and differences between compelled experimental use and voluntary professional adoption. Remote administration could not technologically prevent prohibited AI access. They report no detectable imbalance in observed characteristics after differential attrition, but emphasize that experienced practitioners, broader assignments and other technological configurations may yield different results.
qs: First, law students differ from practicing lawyers in experience, legal knowledge, professional incentives, and exposure to real-world consequences.
Results may differ with different foundation models, models developed specifically for legal use, different prompting strategies, or unstructured AI use.
For these reasons, our results should be understood as evidence about a specific population, task type, time horizon, and technological configuration.

kp.k: Recommendations prioritize independently assessable, narrowly bounded assistance
kp.d: As practice recommendations rather than experimentally established universal rules, the authors advise using AI only where lawyers can independently assess, adapt, explain and build on its output; dividing broad assignments into bounded components through human judgment; and avoiding reliance under severe time pressure or fatigue. They recommend training junior and senior lawyers to evaluate AI suggestions critically, preserving time for verification and independent reasoning.
qs: Senior lawyers must learn to exercise judgment regarding when and how to integrate suggestions from AI, rather than treating AI as infallible.
Junior lawyers must develop the same critical approach.

A second essential principle for using AI without undermining the human user’s independent legal reasoning is to employ it for narrow, well-defined tasks rather than for broad assignments that bundle together multiple analytical steps.
A final principle suggested by our experimental results is that lawyers should avoid using AI to complete legal tasks under artificially tight time constraints or when cognitively fatigued.

kp.k: Future research should vary users, tasks and timescales
kp.d: The authors call for further randomized trials varying doctrine, complexity, incentives and time constraints, including practicing attorneys and participants without legal training. They propose standardized downstream syntheses to separate cognitive effects from better intermediate documents, longer intervals between tasks, and professional field and longitudinal studies. Potential settings include clinics, nonprofit providers and in-house departments, subject to confidentiality, client-protection and selection challenges.
qs: Future randomized controlled trials might also focus on practicing attorneys rather than upper-level law students.
Yet another approach might be to use participants without any legal training to better understand the relationship between AI tools and increasing rates of pro se litigation.

Observational research is also crucial for evaluating the long-term effects of AI use on the development of lawyering skills, although isolating selection effects and accurately measuring distinct patterns of AI use will be challenging.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bednar, Cleveland, Erbsen and Schwarcz argue that AI’s effects on legal work and independent reasoning depend on when and how it is used: initial synthesis assistance improved work quality and subsequent unaided application, whereas AI-assisted revision improved weaker drafts but degraded stronger ones.
pts.d: In their experiment, AI-assisted synthesis increased overall rubric scores by 59.78%, reduced completion time by 12.62%, and increased productivity, defined as rubric points per minute, by 92.36%. Subsequent closed-book comprehension showed no statistically significant difference. On the application task, completed without AI but with access to earlier synthesis memos, the previously AI-exposed group scored 24.01% higher overall; its slightly longer completion time and higher points-per-minute productivity were not statistically significant. The authors interpret the application advantage as operating through stronger synthesis memos rather than demonstrating an independently established improvement in underlying cognitive capacity. At revision, weaker initial memos improved while stronger ones deteriorated, without reversing the general ranking of participants. More broadly, the authors describe a gap between AI’s technical potential and its limited structural impact on the profession as of early 2026, and predict growing potential productivity benefits as models and legal-AI products improve. They recommend independently assessable, narrowly bounded assistance rather than delegation of reasoning that users cannot understand or defend.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a randomized experiment with 91 upper-level law students; broader claims draw on earlier legal experiments, model benchmarks, field-study reports, professional guidance and cross-domain research.
pts.d: The October 2025 experiment analyzed 50 AI-exposed and 41 control participants at the University of Minnesota Law School, using Gemini 2.5 Pro. Participants completed synthesis, comprehension, application and revision tasks about servitudes on personal property. One experienced legal-writing professor graded all 273 anonymized, randomized memos using standardized rubrics. Synthesis quality, speed and productivity differences had p-values below 0.001. Comprehension scores were 3.86 versus 3.88 out of six (p = 0.935); application quality was 5.29 versus 6.56 (p = 0.02); application time and productivity differences had p-values of 0.09 and 0.202. Regression controls for GPA, law-school year and prior AI use did not materially change the central results. Controlling for synthesis quality rendered the AI-exposure coefficient on application quality statistically insignificant, which the authors offer as evidence for an indirect mechanism. Revision findings come from within-participant score changes and regression analysis; all participants used AI at that stage, rather than being randomized to AI versus non-AI revision. Suggested mechanisms—flattening of sophisticated reasoning, fatigue, time pressure and excessive deference—remain interpretations rather than separately established findings. The authors also cite prior student RCTs, the Vals AI evaluation of commercial legal-AI platforms and a legal-aid field study based on perceived productivity improvements. Their longer-term skill-development concerns rely on theory and evidence from other domains, not longitudinal legal evidence from this experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern immediate performance within a single three-hour session under structured, closed-universe, human-in-the-loop conditions; they do not establish the long-term effects of sustained AI reliance.
pts.d: The April 2026 working paper reports an experiment conducted remotely in October 2025. AI was available to the treatment group during the initial synthesis task, unavailable to both groups during comprehension and application, and required for both groups during revision. Task limits were 75, 10, 60 and 20 minutes, respectively. Participants received a curated twelve-page source packet, a hypothetical jurisdiction and structured prompting and checking instructions. The authors explicitly limit generalization beyond one institution, one doctrinal topic, one model and an artificially fragmented assignment. AI prohibitions could not be technologically enforced, and task times were self-reported. Minimal observed fabrication in this setting is not presented as evidence that hallucinations have disappeared or that open-ended legal research is equally reliable. The authors leave open both cumulative skill erosion and improved AI-use proficiency over months or years. Their recommendations to avoid tight deadlines and fatigue are informed by possible explanations for the revision pattern, not a separate experimental comparison of those conditions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct evidence concerns second- and third-year law students, with implications primarily for junior-lawyer work, professional training and supervision; the authors also identify risks for experienced lawyers working beyond their expertise.
pts.d: Students and junior lawyers may produce better foundational work more quickly and then use that work to support subsequent analysis, but AI-assisted revision can undermine already strong drafts. The authors regard newly licensed lawyers as especially vulnerable to developmental harm if AI replaces repeated engagement with difficult materials. Senior lawyers are not exempt when using AI in unfamiliar areas, although experienced practitioners can use existing expertise to assess and adapt suggestions for familiar tasks. Law firms and educators are urged to train critical assessment of AI advice and preserve independent issue identification, analytical structure and judgment. Clients, judges and supervising lawyers are affected when practitioners cannot explain, defend or adapt AI-generated work. The paper does not directly measure client outcomes, employment displacement, pricing or changes to firm staffing. Legal-aid practitioners appear in the supporting literature; untrained users and pro se litigants are proposed populations for future research rather than populations tested here.
